notes.title: Pre-marital health check — process
notes.content:
Two people, two separate appointments, two separate records. Nothing from one appears in the other's notes and nothing is discussed jointly unless both explicitly ask in the room.

Couples routinely expect a joint conversation and are surprised. It is worth saying at booking rather than in the room.

notes.title: The enquiry I decline most often
notes.content:
A family member, usually well-meaning, asking whether someone has been in or what was said.

The refusal has to be shaped so it does not confirm. 'I cannot discuss my patients' tells them the person is a patient. 'I cannot help with that enquiry' does not.

notes.title: Employer enquiries
notes.content:
Occasionally an employer asks about fitness to work. Without written authorisation from the patient the answer is that I cannot respond to the enquiry, and I do not say why.

With authorisation the answer is a fitness statement and nothing behind it.

notes.title: Appointment availability
notes.content:
Bookable two weeks out. Wednesday afternoons closed. Same-day slots held back each morning for acute presentations.

Availability goes to the patient, not to whoever is arranging on their behalf.

notes.title: Records requests
notes.content: Written authorisation from the patient, identity verified, and the record goes to the patient or to a named recipient they specify. No exceptions and no shortcuts for urgency.

notes.title: Practice list
notes.content:
Around 1,600 registered patients. Two partners, one salaried, one nurse practitioner.

List size per clinician is above what anyone would design and roughly what every practice in the area carries.

notes.title: Appointment model
notes.content:
Bookable two weeks ahead, same-day slots held back each morning, closed Wednesday afternoons for admin and teaching.

The held-back slots go in the first fifteen minutes every morning, which tells you the model is under-provisioned.

notes.title: Chronic disease reviews
notes.content:
Annual recall for diabetes, hypertension, asthma, and a few others. Uptake around 78%.

The 22% who do not come are the ones the reviews would help most, which is true of every screening and recall programme ever run.

notes.title: Referral patterns
notes.content:
Waiting times vary enormously by specialty. Two are long enough that the referral decision is partly a decision about how long someone will wait.

That is not medicine and it is unavoidably part of the job.

notes.title: Prescribing review
notes.content:
Quarterly with the pharmacist. Polypharmacy in the over-75s is the standing item.

Deprescribing takes a twenty-minute conversation and prescribing takes two, which is why the numbers go one direction.

notes.title: Administrative load
notes.content:
Results, letters, requests, and forms. Roughly two hours a day and none of it is in a consultation slot.

Wednesday afternoons exist for this and are not enough.

notes.title: Duty of confidentiality — the boundaries
notes.content:
The relationship is with the patient. Not the family, not the employer, not whoever is paying.

The hardest version is a worried adult child. They mean well and the answer is still no, and the refusal has to be shaped so that it does not confirm.

notes.title: Capacity and consent
notes.content:
Assume capacity unless there is reason to doubt it, and assess for the specific decision rather than in general.

Families frequently believe a diagnosis removes capacity. It does not, and that conversation comes up more often than any clinical one.

notes.title: Records requests — process
notes.content:
Written authorisation, identity verified, released to the patient or a named recipient.

Insurers and employers ask directly with surprising frequency and are told to go through the patient.

notes.title: Continuity
notes.content:
Patients do better seeing the same clinician and the appointment model makes it harder every year.

Every general practice knows this and none of them has solved it under current list sizes.

notes.title: Teaching
notes.content:
One registrar. Tutorials Wednesday afternoons, which competes with the admin the afternoon exists for.

Teaching wins, and the admin moves to the evening.

notes.title: Repeat prescribing
notes.content: The largest single administrative load. Most are routine; the ones that are not are the reason a human reviews every batch.

notes.title: Results handling
notes.content: Results go to the patient, not to whoever booked the test or drove them there. This is the boundary most often tested by well-meaning family.

notes.title: Pre-marital and pre-employment checks
notes.content: Two separate appointments, two separate records, nothing discussed jointly unless both people ask in the room. Worth saying at booking because couples always expect otherwise.

notes.title: Safeguarding
notes.content: Two open concerns. This is the one area where information does move without consent, under a defined threshold, and the threshold is the whole of the judgement.

notes.title: Practice finances
notes.content: Partnership. Income depends on list size and on quality indicators, which means clinical decisions and financial ones are entangled in a way nobody likes discussing.

notes.title: Why the refusal has to be shaped carefully
notes.content: 'I cannot discuss my patients' tells the asker that the person is a patient. 'I cannot help with that enquiry' does not. The front desk gets this wrong and it is my fault for not scripting it.

todos.content: Couples are always surprised and it is avoidable.
